name: Peptide stacks (Wolverine stack)

card.summary: BPC-157 plus TB-500, the recovery-peptide pairing; animal data and forum hope, no human appearance trials.
card.note: Not approved by any regulator; banned by WADA; human safety data are insufficient.

quick.overview:
The Wolverine stack pairs BPC-157, a gastric-derived peptide, with TB-500, a thymosin beta-4 fragment. Users describe it for injury recovery, and looksmaxxing forums sometimes extend peptide stacks to skin, bone or height.

Evidence is mostly animal research and a few small human studies; none addresses appearance.
quick.mechanism: In animal studies BPC-157 shows tissue-protective effects and promotes blood-vessel growth; thymosin beta-4 binds actin and promotes cell migration. Human mechanisms are not established.
quick.risks: No regulator has approved BPC-157; health authorities cite insufficient safety data and a theoretical tumour concern. It is WADA-banned. Gray-market products are unregulated.

lead: A peptide stack is a combination of several peptides used together. The best-known recovery pairing is the "Wolverine stack", a nickname for BPC-157 plus TB-500, which proponents link to faster repair of tendons, joints and muscle and to quicker recovery between training sessions.[1][2] The name evokes the fast-healing comic-book character. In looksmaxxing communities, "peptide stack" is also a broader label that can include growth-hormone secretagogues such as CJC-1295 and ipamorelin, the copper peptide GHK-Cu, and weight-loss peptides, discussed for body composition, skin quality, bone mass or height.[3][4][9]

The appearance chain people describe is mostly indirect: recovery peptides are meant to help injuries and sore joints heal so that training can continue, which supports muscle gain and a leaner physique, while GHK-Cu is discussed for skin, and secretagogues for body composition. Teenagers on forums sometimes ask whether stacks might add height or facial bone mass while growth plates or sutures remain open.[3][4]

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide whose discovery was published in 1993 by Predrag Sikirić's group in Zagreb; Wikipedia states that it is not approved by any drug regulator for human use and that human data are scarce.[1] TB-500 is described in anti-doping literature as a synthetic version of an active region of thymosin beta-4, a 44-amino-acid protein studied in cell and animal work and in phase 2 trials of topical and eye products.[2] Two systematic reviews of the human literature on BPC-157 were published in 2025 and 2026.[10][11] No clinical study has tested the BPC-157 plus TB-500 combination, or either peptide, for facial appearance, bone mass or height.

paras: BPC-157, also called body protection compound 157, is derived from a protein found in human gastric juice.[1] Preclinical studies, mostly in rodents, describe cytoprotective, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects and possible acceleration of tissue healing; it promotes blood-vessel formation in animals.[1] Reported elimination half-life in rats after injection was between roughly 8 and 30 minutes, and the peptide has been described as stable in human gastric juice for more than a day.[1] Detection methods for urine tests were published in 2017.[1]

Thymosin beta-4 is a 44-residue protein encoded by the TMSB4X gene. It forms a 1:1 complex with G-actin, buffering actin monomers, and in laboratory studies it promotes cell migration, blood-vessel formation and stem-cell maturation while lowering pro-inflammatory cytokines.[2] TB-500 itself receives little coverage in encyclopedic sources and appears mainly in doping literature as a synthetic version of an active region of the protein.[2]

Other peptides that appear in forum stacks are growth-hormone secretagogues, drugs that stimulate growth-hormone release through the ghrelin (GHSR) or growth-hormone-releasing-hormone receptor. Ipamorelin is listed as a GHSR agonist and CJC-1295 (with or without a DAC modification) as a GHRH receptor agonist; their established clinical role for this drug class is the treatment of growth hormone deficiency, and the class also raises IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol.[9]

The complete sequence of thymosin beta-4 was determined and synthesised in 1981, and the gene was characterised in 1989.[2] Sikirić's group, now emeritus at the University of Zagreb School of Medicine, published BPC-157 in 1993; later milestones in the literature include a rat Achilles tendon study in 2003, a ligament study in 2010, and a preclinical safety evaluation in 2020.[1]

subs.h: Doping cases that publicised thymosin beta-4
paras: In Australia, sports scientist Stephen Dank ran an injection-based supplement program at Essendon from November 2011 that included a substance listed as "thymosin".[7] The Australian Football League tribunal found 34 players not guilty in March 2015, but in January 2016 the Court of Arbitration for Sport, on a World Anti-Doping Agency appeal, found them guilty of using thymosin beta-4 and imposed two-year bans; the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed the players' appeal in October 2016.[7] A separate Cronulla Sharks inquiry in rugby league concerned other peptides, CJC-1295 and GHRP-6, which Dank admitted were injected into players.[8]

Wikipedia says BPC-157 gained popularity among athletes and the general public for injury recovery and that it is used in functional medicine.[1] On looksmax.org, threads from 2025 show users requesting feedback on peptide stacks and posting Wolverine-stack threads, alongside stacks built from secretagogues and GHK-Cu.[3][4][5] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing reports that GHK-Cu has gained virality, that some people inject it from unregulated sources, and that the FDA has warned about the lack of human testing of the injectable form.[6]

Forum threads present stacks as menus: a recovery pair, a secretagogue pair, a copper peptide for skin and sometimes a fat-loss peptide, with posters asking others to critique the combination.[3][4] Typical stated goals include body-fat reduction, clearer or firmer skin, and, among younger posters, height or facial bone mass.[3][4] Replies range from enthusiastic to sceptical; in one thread a respondent says secretagogues release much less growth hormone than the hormone itself and that GHK-Cu mainly helps skin that is already fairly clear.[3]
These are individual reports and opinions. This wiki does not reproduce amounts, schedules or sourcing.

Per Wikipedia, human safety data for BPC-157 are insufficient, health authorities discourage its use, and because it promotes angiogenesis some reviewers raise a theoretical concern that it could promote or enlarge undetected cancers.[1] The 2025 systematic review in HSS Journal reported that no clinical safety data were found and warned of adverse effects from unregulated manufacturing.[10]

WADA added BPC-157 to the prohibited list in 2022 under category S0, and thymosin beta-4 is banned as a recovery aid that may permit heavier training.[1][2] Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (April 2024) and New Zealand's Medsafe (June 2025) moved to control BPC-157 as a prescription medicine, although it is not in practice available by prescription.[1]

In the United States, Wikipedia reports an HHS enforcement-discretion policy dated 10 October 2026 and a 30 October 2026 announcement by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that BPC-157 and five other peptides (TB-500, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c and semax) could be supplied by compounding pharmacies; the peptide remains unapproved by the FDA.[1] The same article lists the approval gap, the cancer concern, the prescription-status contradiction and the fact that much key work comes from the discoverer's own group among the controversies.[1]

No studies found of the BPC-157 plus TB-500 combination. For BPC-157 alone, a 2025 systematic review covering literature to June 2024 included 36 studies, 35 preclinical and one clinical: a retrospective report in which 7 of 12 patients with chronic knee pain reported relief lasting over six months.[10] A 2026 PRISMA-registered review searching to June 2026 found three human studies with 30 participants in total (intra-articular injections for knee pain, an intravesical pilot in interstitial cystitis, and an intravenous safety pilot); most participants reported symptom improvement and no treatment-related adverse events, the studies were of poor methodological quality, certainty was rated very low, and the authors concluded BPC-157 should not be used clinically outside approved high-quality trials.[11] Wikipedia also lists a small 2021 intra-articular study and a phase I trial whose results were not submitted.[1]

Thymosin beta-4 has been studied in phase 2 trials for pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa, reported to speed repair and be well tolerated, and in dry-eye and neurotrophic keratopathy; heart-repair trials are described as ongoing.[2] None of these studies measured facial appearance, bone mass or height.

timeline.event: Complete sequence of thymosin beta-4 determined and synthesised.[2]
Sikirić's group publishes BPC-157 in the Journal of Physiology, Paris.[1]
Rat Achilles tendon study reports accelerated healing with BPC-157.[1]
Stephen Dank's injection program begins at Essendon, including a substance listed as thymosin.[7]
Court of Arbitration for Sport finds 34 Essendon players guilty of thymosin beta-4 use; Swiss Federal Supreme Court upholds the bans in October.[7]
WADA adds BPC-157 to the prohibited list under S0.[1]
Australia's TGA moves to control BPC-157 as a prescription medicine; a first systematic review of orthopaedic use of BPC-157 follows in 2025.[1][10]
New Zealand's Medsafe reviews and controls BPC-157; looksmax.org peptide-stack threads appear.[1][3][4][5]
A second systematic review of human BPC-157 evidence is published (October); on 30 October HHS announces compounding pharmacies may supply BPC-157 and five other peptides.[1][11]

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org discuss peptide stacks as options for recovery, skin, body composition and, among younger posters, height or bone mass; the Wolverine stack is the recovery pairing most often named.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: BPC-157 plus TB-500 (the "Wolverine stack") speeds healing and recovery.
claims.believers: Forum users start threads on the pairing under the Wolverine name and discuss it as a recovery option beside other stacks.[5] Athletes and the general public use BPC-157 mainly for injury recovery.[1]
claims.experts: Evidence is mostly animal studies; a 2025 review found one clinical study of 12 patients and no clinical safety data, and a 2026 review found three small, poor-quality human studies and rated certainty very low.[10][11]

claims.claim: Peptide stacks can add facial bone mass or height in teenagers.
claims.believers: Teen posters ask about stacks while growth plates and sutures are open and some say they would accept the risk.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published study has tested these peptide combinations for facial bone or height in adolescents; a forum reply itself notes that growth hormone raises height in studies only in short-stature or GH-deficient children.[3]

claims.believers: Users say it can help skin, with some noting little effect on young, clear skin.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article reports that injectable GHK-Cu has gone viral and that the FDA has warned about the lack of human testing of the injectable form.[6]

claims.claim: CJC-1295 with ipamorelin raises growth hormone enough to help physique and growth.
claims.believers: Posters include the pair in starter stacks for body composition and growth.[3][4]
claims.experts: Secretagogues are an established drug class for growth hormone deficiency and also raise IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol.[9] CJC-1295 and GHRP-6 were among peptides banned by WADA and linked to the Cronulla case.[8]

claims.claim: Peptides are low-risk because they occur naturally.
claims.believers: Posters weigh peptides against perceived upside when asking for stack feedback, often asking mainly whether a stack will work rather than how safe it is.[3][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says human safety data on BPC-157 are insufficient and notes a theoretical cancer concern linked to angiogenesis; the 2025 review found no clinical safety data and warned of unregulated manufacturing.[1][10]
